# 01-js/05 Modules

**Time:** 25 min lesson, 35 min exercises (core), plus 10 min stretch.

## 1. Watch the lesson

Run `yarn lessons`, open the link it prints, and pick **01-js/05 Modules**.

## 2. Quick recap

- One file is one module. Only names marked `export` can be imported from another file.
- Import your own files with a relative path and the full file name: `import { compute } from './stats.js';`. A bare name like `'axios'` is a package.
- **Named** exports: many per file, imported in braces with the exact name. **Default** export: at most one per file, imported without braces under any name.
- A module runs once, on its first import, and every importer shares it. Imports are live: they always show the current value.
- An `index.js` can re-export a folder's public names, so the rest of the code has one place to import from.

## 3. Exercises

This module is a small folder of files instead of one `exercises.js`. Each step says which file to change.

| Step | Level | File | Task |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | core | [`priorities.js`](priorities.js) | Export `PRIORITIES` and `comparePriority` (named exports) |
| 2 | core | [`format.js`](format.js) | Import `PRIORITIES`, and make `formatTicket` the default export |
| 3 | core | [`tickets.js`](tickets.js) | Move `isOverdue` into a new file `dates.js`, then import it back |
| 4 | core | [`index.js`](index.js) | Re-export all five public names from one place |
| 5 | core | [`counter.js`](counter.js) | Export a `count` variable and an `increment()` function |
| 6 | core | [`report.js`](report.js) | `overdueReport()`, importing only from `./index.js` |
| 7 | stretch | [`report.js`](report.js) | `loadFormatter()`, loading `format.js` on demand with `import()` |

Check all steps:

```
yarn verify 01-js/05
```

Check one step:

```
yarn verify 01-js/05/3
```

Always write the `.js` at the end of your own imports. The checker looks for it, because plain Node (which runs `yarn tickets` in your project) refuses imports without it.

Coming from Python? Step 4 is what a package's `__init__.py` does when it imports names from its submodules.

# 02-ts/08 Migrating JavaScript to TypeScript

**Time:** 20 min lesson, 30 min exercises (core), plus 5 min stretch.

## 1. Watch the lesson

Run `yarn lessons` and pick **02-ts/08 Migrating JavaScript to TypeScript**.

## 2. Quick recap

- Migrate in small steps, keeping the code working after each one.
- `// @ts-check` at the top of a `.js` file makes TypeScript check it with loose settings: it finds real bugs before you change anything.
- Rename one file to `.ts`. Strict mode then asks for parameter types. Answer with real types, imported with `import type` or `import { type X }`.
- Never silence the checker: no `any`, no `as`, no `!`, no `@ts-ignore`. Each of those hides a question TypeScript asked.
- Data from axios is `any` by default. Ask for `unknown` (`client.get<unknown>(...)`) and pass it through a type guard.

## 3. Exercises

You migrate [`report.js`](report.js), a small module that builds an overdue report. [`types.ts`](types.ts) already has the `Ticket` type and an `isTicket` guard for you to import.

| Step | Level | Task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | core | Add `// @ts-check` to `report.js` and fix the bug it finds |
| 2 | core | Rename `report.js` to `report.ts` (behaviour unchanged) |
| 3 | core | Zero type errors under strict |
| 4 | core | No `any`, `as`, `!` or `@ts-ignore` |
| 5 | core | `fetchReport` checks the API data with `isTicket` |
| 6 | stretch | `PRIORITY_WEIGHT` with `as const satisfies` |

```
yarn verify 02-ts/08
```

This is a rehearsal for your Phase 2 project, where you migrate your own Phase 1 code the same way.

# Phase 2 project: ticket logic in strict TypeScript

## Definition of Done

For the user, `yarn tickets` behaves exactly as before. Nothing visible changes; the code is now safe to build on.

Technical:

- [ ] Every Phase 1 file is `.ts`, and `tsc --noEmit` passes with `strict: true`.
- [ ] No `any`, no `@ts-ignore`, no non-null `!` assertions.
- [ ] Ticket statuses and priorities are defined once as `as const` arrays, and their types are derived from them.
- [ ] A ticket is a discriminated union on `status` (for example, only a `closed` ticket has `closedAt`, only an `assigned` ticket has `assignee`).
- [ ] Every `switch` on status is exhaustive, enforced by a `never` check.
- [ ] API responses arrive as `unknown` and pass through a type guard before use; a malformed ticket is reported, not trusted.
- [ ] `yarn verify 02-ts/project` passes.

**Stretch:** the due-date sort from Phase 1 still works (step 9), then template literal types, mapped types, and generic constraints with `extends` wherever they make your code clearer.

**Time:** about 1.5 hours.

## What you are building

The same code as Phase 1, made safe. On day 2 a React app imports it from here, so keep the function names exactly as they are.

```
src/
  constants.ts    STATUSES, PRIORITIES as const, with Status and Priority derived from them
  types.ts        Ticket (a discriminated union), Assignee, and the other shapes    (new file)
  api.ts          client.get<unknown>, then isTicket on every item
  filters.ts      filterTickets, sortTickets
  stats.ts        groupByStatus, computeStats, statusLabel                           (statusLabel is new)
  validation.ts   validateTicket, isTicket                                           (isTicket is new)
  index.ts        re-exports everything, including types.ts
```

## How to work

1. Run `yarn copy-project` once. It copies `01-js/project/src` into `02-ts/project/src`. It never overwrites: if the folder exists, it stops and tells you.
2. Rename every file in `02-ts/project/src` from `.js` to `.ts`, and change the imports to match (`./constants.ts`). Step 1 now passes, and VS Code shows red underlines.
3. Fix one file at a time, in this order. Each one only depends on the files before it, so the errors you see are your own.
   1. **constants.ts:** add `as const` and export `Status` and `Priority` derived from the arrays (module 02-ts/07).
   2. **types.ts and validation.ts:** write the `Ticket` union, one type per status (module 02-ts/05). Then write `isTicket(value: unknown): value is Ticket` next to `validateTicket` (module 02-ts/04).
   3. **filters.ts:** type the parameters. Hover anything you are not sure of.
   4. **stats.ts:** type `groupByStatus` and `computeStats`, then add `statusLabel` with a `never` check in `default` (module 02-ts/05).
   5. **api.ts:** ask axios for `unknown`, keep only the items that pass `isTicket`, and make `loadAll` warn about the others by id (module 02-ts/08 is the same workflow).
4. Run `yarn tickets` after each file. It now runs your TypeScript version (it says so on the first line), so you see at once if something stopped working.
5. Run `yarn verify 02-ts/project` to check everything, or `yarn verify 02-ts/project/5` for one step.

Keep the `Ticket` union on one line that starts with `export type Ticket =`. Step 6 adds a fifth status to a copy of that line to prove your `switch` notices.

`statusLabel` turns a ticket into the text a user sees:

| Ticket | `statusLabel(ticket)` |
| --- | --- |
| open | `Open` |
| assigned to `a1` | `Assigned to a1` |
| blocked, reason "Waiting for design" | `Blocked: Waiting for design` |
| closed at `2026-10-28T12:00:00Z` | `Closed on 2026-10-28` |

To see a malformed ticket reported, stop the server (Ctrl+C) and start it with `python server/server.py --bad-data`. `yarn tickets` should still show every good ticket, plus a warning that names the bad one.

## Steps

| Step | Level | What `yarn verify 02-ts/project/<step>` checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | core | Every file in `src/` is `.ts` |
| 2 | core | `tsc` in strict mode finds no errors in `src/` |
| 3 | core | No `any`, no `as` casts (`as const` is fine), no `!`, no `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-expect-error` |
| 4 | core | `STATUSES` and `PRIORITIES` are `as const`, and `Status` and `Priority` are derived from them |
| 5 | core | `Ticket` is a discriminated union: an open ticket cannot have `closedAt`, an assigned one needs an `assignee` |
| 6 | core | `statusLabel` gives the labels above, and adding a status breaks the build |
| 7 | core | `api.ts` asks for `unknown`, `isTicket` is a type guard, and `loadAll` names the malformed ticket |
| 8 | core | Phase 1 steps 1 to 10 still pass on this version |
| 9 | stretch | Phase 1 step 11 (due-date sort) still passes |

## When you are done

Run `yarn progress`. If every Phase 2 core step is green, day 1 is done. Tomorrow starts with Phase 3's first lesson, and the final project imports this `src` folder.

# Final project: migrate, fix and extend the ticket app

A teammate wrote this ticket tracker in JavaScript. It mostly works, but users report odd behaviour and it feels slow with a lot of tickets. Your job is the kind of ticket you will get in your first weeks: move it to TypeScript, find and fix what is wrong, and add one feature.

## Definition of Done

In the browser, the user can:

- [ ] Open the ticket list and see an antd Table of tickets from the Python API, with a loading state while it fetches and an error state with a Retry button if the server is down.
- [ ] Sort the table by any column and page through results.
- [ ] Filter by status and priority, and type in a search box that only filters after they stop typing (debounced).
- [ ] Filter by assignee, and have that filter kept in the URL: refreshing the page or sharing the link keeps the same filter. *(the new feature)*
- [ ] Click "New ticket" and fill in an antd Form that validates required fields and shows field errors inline.
- [ ] Click a ticket to edit it in the same form, pre-filled; saving updates the table without a manual refresh.
- [ ] Use the browser back and forward buttons between the list and the form pages.
- [ ] Type in the search box without the whole table visibly lagging.

Technical:

- [ ] Every file in `src` is `.ts` or `.tsx`; `tsc` passes with `strict: true` and no `any`.
- [ ] ESLint passes with the React Hooks rules turned on, with no disabled rules.
- [ ] All six Rules of React bugs are fixed (each has its own check).
- [ ] All three performance problems are fixed (each has its own check).
- [ ] The debounced search uses your `useDebouncedValue` hook, in `src/hooks/useDebouncedValue.ts`.
- [ ] `yarn verify final-project` passes.

**Time:** about 3 hours.

## Before you start

The app's ticket logic is **your own Phase 2 project**. Every file here imports it as `@tickets/logic`, which points at `02-ts/project/src/index.ts`. So `filterTickets`, `sortTickets`, `computeStats`, `statusLabel`, `isTicket` and the `Ticket` type are the ones you wrote yesterday. If your Phase 2 project is not green yet, ask your mentor.

## Run it

Terminal 1, the API:

```
python server/server.py
```

Terminal 2, the app:

```
yarn dev final-project
```

Try the app with the server in different moods (stop it with Ctrl+C and start it again with an option):

| Start the server with | To see |
| --- | --- |
| `--delay 1500` | The loading state |
| `--fail tickets` | The error state and the Retry button |
| `--many 2000` | Whether typing in the search still feels instant |

## What is in `src`

```
main.jsx                    providers: React Query, antd theme and App, the router
App.jsx                     the routes: /tickets, /tickets/new, /tickets/:id
api/client.js               the axios client (createClient from your Phase 2 logic)
api/tickets.js              useTickets, useTicket, useAssignees, useSaveTicket (React Query)
pages/TicketListPage.jsx    the list: stats, filters, table
pages/TicketFormPage.jsx    create and edit
components/                 TicketTable, TicketFilters, StatsPanel, TicketForm
```

## How to work

1. Click around with the server in each mood above. Note anything that looks wrong.
2. Run `yarn verify final-project`. Each failing step names a symptom, not the fix. Run one step with `yarn verify final-project/7`.
3. Migrate to TypeScript one file at a time (step 1), starting with `api/`, then `components/`, then `pages/`. The bug steps run on `.js` and `.ts` alike, so you can fix bugs before, during or after the migration.
4. ESLint (step 3) points at some of the bugs on its own. Read each rule's message before you change anything.
5. For the performance steps, module 03-react/07 shows how to count renders and read the browser's Performance tab.

## Steps

| Step | What `yarn verify final-project/<step>` checks |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Every file in `src` is `.ts` or `.tsx` |
| 2 | `tsc` passes in strict mode, with no `any` |
| 3 | ESLint passes, including the React Hooks rules |
| 4 to 9 | One Rules of React bug each. The check describes what the user would see. |
| 10 to 12 | One performance problem each, measured while typing in the search box |
| 13 | The assignee filter, kept in the URL as `?assignee=a3` |

## When you are done

Every core step in `yarn progress` is green. Show your mentor the app running with `--many 2000`, and walk them through one bug: what the user saw, why it happened, and what rule of React it broke.

# 02-ts/08 Migrating JavaScript to TypeScript

**Time:** 10 min lesson, 20 min exercises (core), plus 5 min stretch.

## 1. Watch the lesson

Run `yarn lessons` and pick **02-ts/08 Migrating JavaScript to TypeScript**.

## 2. Quick recap

- Migrate in small steps, keeping the code working after each one.
- `// @ts-check` at the top of a `.js` file makes TypeScript check it with loose settings: it finds real bugs before you change anything.
- Rename one file to `.ts`. Strict mode then asks for parameter types. Answer with real types, imported with `import type` or `import { type X }`.
- Never silence the checker: no `any`, no `as`, no `!`, no `@ts-ignore`. Each of those hides a question TypeScript asked.
- Data from axios is `any` by default. Ask for `unknown` (`client.get<unknown>(...)`) and pass it through a type guard.

## 3. Exercises

You migrate [`report.js`](report.js), a small module that builds an overdue report. [`types.ts`](types.ts) already has the `Ticket` type and an `isTicket` guard for you to import.

| Step | Level | Task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | core | Add `// @ts-check` to `report.js` and fix the bug it finds |
| 2 | core | Rename `report.js` to `report.ts` (behaviour unchanged) |
| 3 | core | Zero type errors under strict |
| 4 | core | No `any`, `as`, `!` or `@ts-ignore` |
| 5 | core | `fetchReport` checks the API data with `isTicket` |
| 6 | stretch | `PRIORITY_WEIGHT` with `as const satisfies` |

```
yarn verify 02-ts/08
```

# Phase 2 project: ticket logic in strict TypeScript

**Time:** about 2 to 2.5 hours. **Before you start:** the Phase 1 project and every core step of modules 02-ts/01 to 02-ts/08 are green in `yarn progress`.

## What you are building

The same code as Phase 1, made safe. You copy your Phase 1 project, rename every file to `.ts`, and answer every question strict TypeScript asks, without switching the checker off. Two things are new: the API's answer is checked before it is trusted, and a ticket's type knows which fields each status has.

For the user, nothing changes: `yarn tickets` prints the same thing as before. In the final project a React app imports this code, so keep the function names exactly as they are.

## Definition of Done

For the user, `yarn tickets` behaves exactly as before. Nothing visible changes; the code is now safe to build on.

Technical:

- [ ] Every Phase 1 file is `.ts`, and strict TypeScript finds no errors in it (`yarn verify 02-ts/project/2`).
- [ ] No `any`, no `@ts-ignore`, no non-null `!` assertions.
- [ ] Ticket statuses and priorities are defined once as `as const` arrays, and their types are derived from them.
- [ ] A ticket is a discriminated union on `status` (for example, only a `closed` ticket has `closedAt`, only an `assigned` ticket has `assignee`).
- [ ] Every `switch` on status is exhaustive, enforced by a `never` check.
- [ ] API responses arrive as `unknown` and pass through a type guard before use; a malformed ticket is reported, not trusted.
- [ ] `yarn verify 02-ts/project` passes.

**Stretch:** the due-date sort from Phase 1 still works (step 9), then template literal types, mapped types, and generic constraints with `extends` wherever they make your code clearer.

## The files

```
src/
  constants.ts    STATUSES, PRIORITIES as const, with Status and Priority derived from them
  types.ts        Ticket (a discriminated union), Assignee, and the other shapes    (new file)
  api.ts          client.get<unknown>, then isTicket on every item
  filters.ts      filterTickets, sortTickets
  stats.ts        groupByStatus, computeStats, statusLabel                           (statusLabel is new)
  validation.ts   validateTicket, isTicket                                           (isTicket is new)
  index.ts        re-exports everything, including types.ts
```

## How to run it

You need two terminals, both in the `bootcamp` folder.

1. Terminal 1, the API. Start it and leave it running: `python server/server.py`.
2. Terminal 2, once: `yarn copy-project`. It copies `01-js/project/src` into `02-ts/project/src`. It never overwrites: if the folder exists, it stops and tells you.
3. Terminal 2, as often as you like: `yarn tickets`. As soon as `02-ts/project/src/index.ts` exists, it runs your TypeScript version instead of the Phase 1 one, and says so on the first line.

To see a malformed ticket reported, stop the API with Ctrl+C and start it with `python server/server.py --bad-data`. The last ticket it sends has a number where the priority should be.

## How to test it

- `yarn verify 02-ts/project` checks every step. `yarn verify 02-ts/project/5` checks one.
- Step 2 runs the TypeScript checker on your `src` folder only. Untouched stretch exercises elsewhere never fail it.
- Step 8 runs the Phase 1 checks again on your TypeScript code, so you know the migration changed nothing for the user.
- VS Code shows the same type errors as red underlines while you type. Hover one to read it.

| Step | Level | What `yarn verify 02-ts/project/<step>` checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | core | Every file in `src/` is `.ts` |
| 2 | core | `tsc` in strict mode finds no errors in `src/` |
| 3 | core | No `any`, no `as` casts (`as const` is fine), no `!`, no `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-expect-error` |
| 4 | core | `STATUSES` and `PRIORITIES` are `as const`, and `Status` and `Priority` are derived from them |
| 5 | core | `Ticket` is a discriminated union: an open ticket cannot have `closedAt`, an assigned one needs an `assignee` |
| 6 | core | `statusLabel` gives the labels above, and adding a status breaks the build |
| 7 | core | `api.ts` asks for `unknown`, `isTicket` is a type guard, and `loadAll` names the malformed ticket |
| 8 | core | Phase 1 steps 1 to 10 still pass on this version |
| 9 | stretch | Phase 1 step 11 (due-date sort) still passes |

## What to expect

**Right after `yarn copy-project`**, step 1 lists your `.js` files, and every other core step says "Finish step 1 first":

```
  ✗  1 core    Every file is .ts
                Still JavaScript: api.js, constants.js, filters.js, index.js, stats.js, validation.js. Rename each one in 02-ts/project/src to .ts.
  ✗  2 core    tsc strict: zero errors
                Finish step 1 first. Not .ts yet: src/constants, src/api, src/filters, src/stats, src/validation, src/index
```

**After the renames**, VS Code fills with red underlines, and step 2 lists the same errors. That is expected: work through them one file at a time (see How to work below).

**When you are done**, `yarn tickets` looks exactly like Phase 1, with two differences. The first line says it runs TypeScript, and a new section shows `statusLabel`:

```
Using 02-ts/project/src/index.ts (TypeScript)

Loading tickets and assignees (loadAll)
  40 tickets, 6 assignees
...
One ticket per status (statusLabel)
  t1     Open
  t2     Assigned to a1
  t3     Blocked: Waiting for design
  t4     Closed on 2026-07-28
```

With the API started with `--bad-data`, every good ticket still loads, and the bad one is named:

```
Loading tickets and assignees (loadAll)
  40 tickets, 6 assignees
  Warning: Skipped 1 malformed ticket(s): t-bad
```

## How to work

1. Run `yarn copy-project` once. It copies `01-js/project/src` into `02-ts/project/src`. It never overwrites: if the folder exists, it stops and tells you.
2. Rename every file in `02-ts/project/src` from `.js` to `.ts`, and change the imports to match (`./constants.ts`). Step 1 now passes, and VS Code shows red underlines.
3. Fix one file at a time, in this order. Each one only depends on the files before it, so the errors you see are your own.
   1. **constants.ts:** add `as const` and export `Status` and `Priority` derived from the arrays (module 02-ts/07).
   2. **types.ts and validation.ts:** write the `Ticket` union, one type per status (module 02-ts/05). The API's tickets also have an optional description, so add `description?: string` to the shared base. Then write `isTicket(value: unknown): value is Ticket` next to `validateTicket` (module 02-ts/04). `validateTicket` checks what a user typed, which can be anything, so give its draft unknown fields: `type TicketDraft = { title?: unknown; priority?: unknown; dueDate?: unknown }`.
   3. **filters.ts:** type the parameters. Hover anything you are not sure of. Only some kinds of ticket have an `assignee`, so `t.assignee` is an error on the union: check `'assignee' in t && t.assignee === filters.assignee`.
   4. **stats.ts:** type `groupByStatus` and `computeStats`, then add `statusLabel` with a `never` check in `default` (module 02-ts/05). Two errors you will likely meet:
      - `reduce` cannot guess its result type from `Object.fromEntries(...)`, which always has string keys. Give it the type and a literal start value: `tickets.reduce<Record<Status, Ticket[]>>((groups, t) => ..., { open: [], assigned: [], blocked: [], closed: [] })`.
      - TypeScript does not let you subtract two `Date`s. Subtract numbers: `now.getTime() - new Date(t.createdAt).getTime()`.
   5. **api.ts:** ask axios for `unknown` and keep only the items that pass `isTicket` (module 02-ts/08 is the same workflow). Then:
      - Keep `fetchTickets(client)` returning `Promise<Ticket[]>`, the valid tickets only: the final project calls it.
      - Write a helper that both `fetchTickets` and `loadAll` use, which returns the valid tickets and the ids of the others: `{ tickets: Ticket[]; invalidIds: string[] }`.
      - In `loadAll`, add a warning that names them, for example `Skipped 1 malformed ticket(s): t-bad`.
      - The error in a `catch` or a rejected promise is `unknown`, and `as` is not allowed. Narrow it: `axios.isAxiosError(error)` tells you it is an axios error (then `error.response?.status` is typed), and `error instanceof Error` gives you `error.message` for anything else.
4. After each file, run `yarn tickets` to see that nothing stopped working, and `yarn verify 02-ts/project` to see which steps pass.

Keep the `Ticket` union on one line that starts with `export type Ticket =`. Step 6 adds a fifth status to a copy of that line to prove your `switch` notices.

`statusLabel` turns a ticket into the text a user sees:

| Ticket | `statusLabel(ticket)` |
| --- | --- |
| open | `Open` |
| assigned to `a1` | `Assigned to a1` |
| blocked, reason "Waiting for design" | `Blocked: Waiting for design` |
| closed at `2026-10-28T12:00:00Z` | `Closed on 2026-10-28` |

## What the final project imports

The final project's React app imports these from your `src/index.ts`. Keep these names and shapes, and the app runs on your code without changes:

| Export | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| `STATUSES`, `PRIORITIES` | the `as const` arrays, and the `Status`, `Priority` types |
| `Ticket`, `Assignee` | your types |
| `createClient(baseURL)` | returns an `AxiosInstance` |
| `fetchTickets(client)` | `Promise<Ticket[]>`, the valid tickets only |
| `fetchAssignees(client)` | `Promise<Assignee[]>` |
| `isTicket(value)` | `value is Ticket` |
| `filterTickets(tickets, { status, priority, assignee, search })` | `Ticket[]` |
| `sortTickets(tickets, { by, direction })` | `Ticket[]`, with `by` one of `'title'`, `'priority'`, `'createdAt'` |
| `computeStats(tickets)` | `{ total, open, overdue, averageAgeDays }` |
| `statusLabel(ticket)` | `string` |

Name the types of the filter, sort and stats objects as you like: you import them by your own names when you migrate the app.

## When you are done

Run `yarn progress`. When every Phase 2 core step is green, Phase 2 is done. Next is Phase 3's first lesson. The final project imports this `src` folder.

# Final project: migrate, fix and extend the ticket app

**Time:** about 4.5 hours. **Before you start:** every core step of Phase 3 is green in `yarn progress`, and so is your Phase 2 project (this app runs on it, see below).

## What you are building

A teammate wrote this ticket tracker in React and JavaScript. It mostly works, but users report odd behaviour and it feels slow with a lot of tickets. Your job is the kind of ticket you will get in your first weeks:

1. **Migrate** it to strict TypeScript.
2. **Fix** six bugs that break the Rules of React, and three performance problems.
3. **Extend** it with one feature: an assignee filter that is kept in the URL.

The app's ticket logic is **your own Phase 2 project**. Every file here imports it as `@tickets/logic`, which points at `02-ts/project/src/index.ts`. So `filterTickets`, `sortTickets`, `computeStats`, `statusLabel`, `isTicket` and the `Ticket` type are the ones you wrote. If your Phase 2 project is not green yet, the app does not start: ask your mentor.

## Definition of Done

In the browser, the user can:

- [ ] Open the ticket list and see an antd Table of tickets from the Python API, with a loading state while it fetches and an error state with a Retry button if the server is down.
- [ ] Sort the table by title, priority or created date, and page through results.
- [ ] Filter by status and priority, and type in a search box that only filters after they stop typing (debounced).
- [ ] Filter by assignee, and have that filter kept in the URL: refreshing the page or sharing the link keeps the same filter. *(the new feature)*
- [ ] Click "New ticket" and fill in an antd Form that validates required fields and shows field errors inline.
- [ ] Click a ticket to edit it in the same form, pre-filled; saving updates the table without a manual refresh.
- [ ] Use the browser back and forward buttons between the list and the form pages.
- [ ] Type in the search box without the whole table visibly lagging.

Technical:

- [ ] Every file in `src` is `.ts` or `.tsx`; `tsc` passes with `strict: true` and no `any`.
- [ ] ESLint passes with the React Hooks rules turned on, with no disabled rules.
- [ ] All six Rules of React bugs are fixed (each has its own check).
- [ ] All three performance problems are fixed (each has its own check).
- [ ] The debounced search uses your `useDebouncedValue` hook, in `src/hooks/useDebouncedValue.ts`.
- [ ] `yarn verify final-project` passes.

## The files

```
src/
  main.jsx                    providers: React Query, antd theme and App, the router
  App.jsx                     the routes: /tickets, /tickets/new, /tickets/:id
  api/client.js               the axios client (createClient from your Phase 2 logic)
  api/tickets.js              useTickets, useTicket, useAssignees, useSaveTicket (React Query)
  pages/TicketListPage.jsx    the list: stats, filters, table
  pages/TicketFormPage.jsx    create and edit
  components/                 TicketTable, TicketFilters, StatsPanel, TicketForm
  hooks/                      does not exist yet: your useDebouncedValue goes here
```

## How to run it

You need two terminals, both in the `bootcamp` folder.

1. Terminal 1, the API: `python server/server.py` (or `py server/server.py`). Leave it running.
2. Terminal 2, the app: `yarn dev final-project`. Open the address it prints, usually http://localhost:5173.

The page reloads by itself when you save a file, so keep it open while you work.

Try the app with the server in different moods. Stop it with Ctrl+C and start it again with an option:

| Start the server with | To see |
| --- | --- |
| `--delay 1500` | The loading state |
| `--fail tickets` | The error state and the Retry button |
| `--many 2000` | Whether typing in the search still feels instant |

## How to test it

- `yarn verify final-project` runs every step. `yarn verify final-project/7` runs only step 7.
- Each failing step describes what the user would see, not the fix. The hint names the module that explains it.
- The bug and performance steps (4 to 13) drive the real app in a test browser, so they work on `.jsx` and `.tsx` alike. You can fix bugs before, during or after the migration.
- Step 3 ignores `eslint-disable` comments. Fix the code, never the rule.
- `yarn tsc -p final-project` and `yarn eslint final-project` show every error with its file and line. VS Code shows the same ones as you type.

| Step | What `yarn verify final-project/<step>` checks |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Every file in `src` is `.ts` or `.tsx` |
| 2 | `tsc` passes in strict mode, with no `any` |
| 3 | ESLint passes, including the React Hooks rules |
| 4 to 9 | One Rules of React bug each. The check describes what the user would see. |
| 10 to 12 | One performance problem each, measured while typing in the search box |
| 13 | The assignee filter, kept in the URL as `?assignee=a3` |

## What to expect

**In the browser**, the app starts and looks finished: a stats panel, filters and a table of 40 tickets. The problems show up when you use it. Some filters do not seem to do anything, the form does not always show the ticket you clicked, and with `--many 2000` the search lags. Click around for ten minutes before you change any code, and write down what looks wrong.

**In `yarn verify`**, every step fails at first. Each message is a symptom you can reproduce in the browser:

```
  ✗  1 core    Every file in src is .ts or .tsx
                10 files are still JavaScript: src/App.jsx, src/api/client.js, ...
  ✗  3 core    ESLint passes with the React Hooks rules
                42:48  error  React Hook "useTicket" is called conditionally ...
  ✗  4 core    Bug: sorting must not change the cached tickets
                The tickets in the React Query cache changed order (now t3, t8, t12, t9, ...).
                Something sorted them in place.
  ✗  7 core    Bug: Previous / Next shows the right ticket in the form
                After going from t1 to t2 (the Next button), the form shows
                "Login page shows blank screen" instead of "Export to CSV drops last row"
  ✗ 11 core    Performance: the list is not filtered again on every render
                While typing 5 letters, the whole list was filtered or sorted again 5 times;
                expected at most 2.
  ✗ 13 core    Feature: assignee filter kept in the URL
                For ?assignee=a3 the table should show a3's 3 tickets, but it shows 10 rows

0 of 13 core steps pass. Next: step 1, Every file in src is .ts or .tsx.
```

If steps 4 to 13 say "02-ts/project/src/index.ts is missing", your Phase 2 project is not in place yet.

Expect step 2 to report many errors right after you rename a file. That is normal: rename one file, fix it, then the next.

**When you are done**, the same command ends with:

```
All 13 core steps pass. Stretch steps are optional.
```

In the browser, the search waits until you stop typing, Previous and Next show the right ticket, and `/tickets?assignee=a3` still shows a3's tickets after you press F5.

## How to work

1. Click around with the server in each mood above. Note anything that looks wrong.
2. Run `yarn verify final-project`. Match each failing step to something you saw in the browser.
3. Migrate to TypeScript one file at a time (step 1), starting with `api/`, then `components/`, then `pages/`.
4. ESLint (step 3) points at some of the bugs on its own. Read each rule's message before you change anything.
5. For the performance steps, module 03-react/07 shows how to count renders and read the browser's Performance tab.
6. Add the feature (step 13) last, once the filters it sits next to work.

Stuck for more than 20 minutes on one step? Ask your mentor, with the step number and the `yarn verify` output.

## TypeScript with antd

Most of step 2's errors come from antd's props. These are the types you will need, all imported from `antd` (`import { type TableColumnsType } from 'antd'`):

| For | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Table columns | `const columns: TableColumnsType<Ticket> = [...]`: then `render: (_, t) => ...` knows `t` is a `Ticket` |
| Table `onChange` | `const handleChange: TableProps<Ticket>['onChange'] = (pagination, filters, sorter) => ...`. `sorter` can be an array, and `sorter.columnKey` is a `Key`, so check it with a type guard before you use it as a sort field. |
| A column's `sortOrder` | `'ascend' \| 'descend' \| null`, not `string` |
| A form | `const [form] = Form.useForm<Values>()`, with `Values` the type of the form's fields |
| `form.setFields` | each `name` must be one of the form's field names (`keyof Values`), not any `string`. A type guard turns the server's field name into one. |
| A ref to an antd `Input` | `useRef<InputRef>(null)` |
| `document.getElementById('root')` | `HTMLElement \| null`: check it with an `if` and throw a clear error |

Step 2 only bans `any` and `@ts-ignore`. Avoid `as` and `!` too, as in Phase 2: each one tells TypeScript to trust you instead of checking. If you keep one, be ready to explain it to your mentor.

## When you are done

Every core step in `yarn progress` is green. Show your mentor the app running with `--many 2000`, and walk them through one bug: what the user saw, why it happened, and what rule of React it broke.
